$comment: verdict: false (not supported by the record) | true (supported) | nuanced (mixed: the record supports part of the claim, or the answer depends on the product, its settings or which evidence is weighed). Each claim is put the way it is usually made. part links to components.json ids, hop to dataflow.json ids.

myths.claim: It does facial recognition.
myths.nuance: Flock says its system does not use facial recognition, and none of the records cited here shows a Flock product identifying a face. Flock's Condor video cameras do detect and follow people: in June 2026, an InvestigateTV reporter filmed a Condor panning and tilting to keep him in frame, and a Flock representative said the camera was not built to track people.

myths.claim: It records video of everyone.
myths.nuance: A Falcon captures six to 12 still frames when its motion sensor triggers; it does not stream or store video. Condor video cameras stream live video. Raven, an acoustic sensor, analyzes short windows of audio. Which of these applies depends on the product installed.

myths.claim: It measures vehicle speed.
myths.nuance: Flock's FAQ says its cameras do not have speed-detection capabilities, and Jalopnik reported that they “do not currently” measure speed. Flock also sells trailers that pair a plate reader with a speed sign, so the answer depends on the product.

myths.claim: It reads phone identifiers.
myths.nuance: No teardown or document shows a Falcon capturing phone identifiers. Its Wi-Fi and Bluetooth radios are documented for installation and battery telemetry. Phone-signal capture products are sold by other vendors.

myths.claim: Only the local agency can see the data.
myths.nuance: Sharing between agencies is part of the platform architecture. The audit log of a Johnson County, Tex., search on May 9, 2025, lists 83,345 cameras in 6,809 networks. Flock told Congress that about 75 percent of law-enforcement customers had opted into the national lookup. Flock removed federal agencies and three states from the lookup in 2025.

myths.claim: The data is kept forever.
myths.nuance: Since Aug. 13, 2026, Flock's default for new customers is seven days, down from 30; existing customers keep the periods they set, and agencies can configure longer ones. Virginia and Washington require deletion after 21 days and California limits its Highway Patrol to 60, unless the data is needed for an investigation. Flock's Evidence Mode keeps selected data with no published limit.

myths.claim: Flock sells customer data.
myths.nuance: Flock states it has never sold customer data. Its terms dated Feb. 16, 2026, no longer contain the clause “Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data” and add a perpetual license to use customer data, the A.C.L.U. found. Flock describes the change as a clarification.

myths.claim: They are only at intersections.
myths.nuance: Flock's product page describes cameras for “high-speed, multi-lane, and off-shoulder roadways,” and the company sells portable Flex units and camera trailers.

myths.claim: It is recording 24/7 and uploading everything.
myths.nuance: Capture is triggered by motion: a passing vehicle produces still images, which Flock's policy says are transferred to its cloud, rather than a continuous video stream. The sensor works day and night, so the difference is in how the vehicles are recorded, not in which ones.

myths.claim: Drivers can opt out.
myths.nuance: No driver-facing opt-out is documented. An agency can add plates to its own safelist, which affects that agency's instance; reads captured by other networks remain searchable in those networks.

myths.claim: A plate cover or spray defeats it.
myths.nuance: The system records a description of each vehicle as well as its plate, and Flock's data sheet and a 2023 sales presentation list missing and covered plates among the attributes it records.

myths.claim: It cannot read temporary paper tags.
myths.nuance: Flock's Falcon Flex data sheet lists paper plates among the plate types it records (“state, partial, paper, and none”). The verdict rests on Flock's description; no independent test is published.

myths.claim: It reads plates and nothing else.
myths.nuance: Flock's own materials list make, type, color, missing or covered plates, roof racks, back racks, trailer hitches, aftermarket wheels, bumper stickers and decals as recorded attributes, and The Texas Tribune reports that the cameras also record dents. Investigators can search those descriptions in natural language.

myths.claim: The city owns the cameras.
myths.nuance: Flock owns the hardware and leases it, at a list price of $3,000 per camera per year; its agreement provides for removal after a contract ends. In Cambridge, Mass., Flock installed two cameras after the city ordered its cameras taken down, and the city then ended the contract; in Evanston, Ill., Flock reinstalled cameras after the city ended its contract; in Verona, Wis., cameras stayed up for months after the contract ended. Cameras that businesses or homeowners' associations pay for are not covered by a city's decision.

myths.claim: An A.I. decides who is a criminal.
myths.nuance: Alerts are generated by matching a plate read against hot lists maintained by agencies; an officer acts on the alert. In Roseville, Calif., 71 percent of stolen-vehicle and felony alerts in 2023 and 2024 involved a misread plate; Flock called the figure a mischaracterization. In Los Angeles, where the readers are Axon units in patrol cars, an inspector general's review counted 161 alerts in two months that were correct reads of cars that, it turned out, were not stolen, from list entries that were not updated in time. The A.C.L.U. has cited cases in which plate-reader errors led to people being held at gunpoint.

myths.claim: Federal agencies have had access to the data.
myths.nuance: Flock states it has no contract with ICE. Audit logs obtained by 404 Media in 2025 show more than 4,000 lookups that local agencies ran for federal agencies or at their request, some listing “ICE” or “immigration” as the reason, and Customs and Border Protection, Homeland Security Investigations, the Secret Service and the Naval Criminal Investigative Service held pilot access. The Illinois secretary of state found that sharing violated state law. In 2025, Flock removed federal agencies from its national lookup and added a setting that controls sharing with them.

myths.claim: Police need a warrant to search it.
myths.nuance: Searches run without a warrant or court order. Flock said in August 2026 that it would require a case number for every law enforcement search by the end of the year, with an exception for emergencies; the number is typed in, not checked. A federal district court in Norfolk, Va., held in 2026 that the network there was not extensive enough to constitute a Fourth Amendment search; the case is on appeal.

myths.claim: Flock has never been hacked.
myths.nuance: No theft of customer data by an attacker is documented. In December 2025 and January 2026, researchers found more than 60 of Flock's Condor video cameras reachable from the internet without a password, exposing live feeds and archives; one researcher said some plate readers were among them. Flock said only Condor cameras were affected and attributed the exposure to carrier testing.

myths.claim: It is proven to reduce crime.
myths.nuance: No peer-reviewed study across many agencies has been published. A working paper by two University of South Carolina criminologists, using deployment records Flock supplied, estimated that reported vehicle thefts fell 11 percent in the year after an agency's first camera went live, when agencies with more thefts beforehand count for more; weighted by population, or with every agency-month counted equally, the change could not be told apart from zero, a point the Institute for Justice made. Forbes reported that burglaries rose in San Marino, Calif., a city Flock had cited for an 80 percent drop. Agencies document recovered vehicles and cleared cases; independent attribution of crime-rate changes to the cameras has not been established.

myths.claim: It does not build a profile of anyone's movements.
myths.nuance: Flock's chief information security officer told the Oshkosh, Wis., council that the system creates no pattern or heat map of an individual's movement. Flock's platform documentation shows a plate search returning every camera that read the vehicle across the retention window, plotted on a map.

myths.claim: Canceling Flock ends plate reading in the area.
myths.nuance: The Finding Flock tracker lists 45 verified decisions from August 2025 to September 2026 to cancel (23), not renew (11), pause (6), deactivate (4) or reject (1) a Flock contract; it is not exhaustive. 404 Media reported that a handful of cities replaced Flock with Axon plate readers; in Denver, privately contracted Flock cameras kept running after the city's contract ended.
